name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Presence of cuticle across different plant organs

questiontext.text: A waxy thick layer called cuticle covers the outer surface of the epidermis to prevent water loss. In which of the following plant organs is the cuticle completely absent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Cuticle Function and Distribution
The epidermis is often covered on the outer surface by a thick waxy layer known as the cuticle, whose primary role is to restrict water loss due to transpiration.

Step 2: Organ-Specific Absence
In roots, the epidermis (epiblema) is specialised for absorbing water and dissolved minerals from the soil. The presence of an impermeable waxy cuticle would impede water uptake; hence, the cuticle is entirely absent in roots.

Final Answer:
The cuticle is absent in roots.

answer.text: Roots
Stems
Dorsiventral leaves
Isobilateral leaves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Shape of guard cells in grasses

questiontext.text: In grasses, the guard cells enclosing the stomatal pore possess which characteristic shape?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stomatal Morphology in Typical Angiosperms
In most dicotyledonous plants, each stoma is bounded by two bean-shaped or kidney-shaped guard cells.

Step 2: Stomatal Variation in Grasses
In monocotyledonous grasses, the guard cells undergo structural modification and are characteristically dumb-bell shaped.

Final Answer:
Guard cells in grasses are dumb-bell shaped.

answer.text: Bean-shaped
Dumb-bell shaped
Kidney-shaped
Barrel-shaped

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Differential wall thickening in stomatal guard cells

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the differential thickening of the cell walls in stomatal guard cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Design of Guard Cells
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells that regulate stomatal opening and closing through turgor changes.

Step 2: Wall Thickness Pattern
The outer walls of the guard cells (directed away from the stomatal aperture) are thin and elastic, whereas the inner walls (directed towards the stomatal pore) are highly thickened and inelastic. This uneven wall thickening causes the cells to bow outward upon becoming turgid, thereby opening the pore.

Final Answer:
The outer walls away from the stomatal pore are thin, while the inner walls facing the stomatal pore are highly thickened.

answer.text: Outer walls away from the pore are highly thickened, while inner walls towards the pore are thin
Both outer and inner walls are uniformly thin to facilitate rapid osmotic swelling
Outer walls away from the pore are thin, while inner walls towards the pore are highly thickened
Both outer and inner walls are uniformly thickened with lignin deposits

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Constituents of the stomatal apparatus

questiontext.text: The stomatal apparatus in flowering plants is collectively composed of which of the following structures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Stomatal Apparatus
The epidermal system on leaves includes specialised stomata for gas exchange and transpiration.

Step 2: Identifying the Components
The stomatal pore (aperture), the pair of enclosing guard cells, and the specialised adjacent epidermal cells termed subsidiary cells together constitute the stomatal apparatus.

Final Answer:
The stomatal apparatus comprises the stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells.

answer.text: Stomatal aperture, trichomes, and cuticle
Guard cells, bulliform cells, and epidermal cells
Stomatal aperture, palisade parenchyma, and guard cells
Stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Nature and role of subsidiary cells

questiontext.text: Subsidiary cells associated with the stomatal apparatus represent:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Origin of Subsidiary Cells
Subsidiary cells belong to the epidermal tissue system of the plant body.

Step 2: Morphological Specialisation
They are specialised epidermal cells located in immediate proximity to the guard cells, displaying distinct alterations in shape and size compared to standard epidermal cells, and assisting in stomatal mechanics.

Final Answer:
Subsidiary cells are specialised epidermal cells in the vicinity of guard cells that differ in shape and size.

answer.text: Specialised epidermal cells in the vicinity of guard cells that differ in shape and size
Modified mesophyll cells that directly provide glucose to guard cells
Endodermal cells with suberised Casparian strips regulating water entry
Sclerenchymatous hypodermal cells providing rigidity to the stomatal pore

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Structural comparison between root hairs and trichomes

questiontext.text: Regarding epidermal appendages, which of the following statements correctly distinguishes root hairs from trichomes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Features of Root Hairs
Root hairs arise as unicellular tubular extensions of the epiblema cells in the root, functioning in the absorption of water and minerals from soil.

Step 2: Features of Trichomes
Trichomes are epidermal appendages present on the shoot system. They are typically multicellular, can be branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, or secretory, and primarily aid in preventing transpirational water loss.

Final Answer:
Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epidermal cells, whereas shoot trichomes are usually multicellular.

answer.text: Root hairs are multicellular and branched, whereas trichomes are always unicellular and stiff
Root hairs are unicellular elongations, whereas trichomes in the shoot system are usually multicellular
Root hairs prevent transpirational water loss, whereas trichomes absorb water from soil
Both root hairs and trichomes are always unicellular and secretory in nature

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Primary physiological function of shoot trichomes

questiontext.text: What is the primary function of trichomes present on the shoot system of plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Trichomes
Trichomes are epidermal hairs distributed on the stems and leaves of the shoot system.

Step 2: Functional Role
By creating a boundary layer that reduces air currents over the epidermal surface, trichomes help prevent excessive water loss caused by transpiration.

Final Answer:
Trichomes assist in preventing water loss due to transpiration.

answer.text: Absorbing capillary water and dissolved solutes from the soil
Forming secondary xylem and phloem during lateral growth
Preventing water loss due to transpiration
Storing starch grains as an energy reservoir

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Cytological characteristics of epidermal cells

questiontext.text: Which of the following cellular features correctly characterizes the parenchymatous cells of the plant epidermis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Epidermal Tissue Characteristics
The epidermis forms the outermost continuous boundary of the primary plant body and is composed of living parenchymatous cells.

Step 2: Cytological Organization
These cells are elongated and compactly placed without intercellular spaces. Internally, each cell possesses a large central vacuole surrounded by a peripheral layer of cytoplasm lining the cell wall.

Final Answer:
Epidermal cells are elongated, compactly arranged parenchymatous cells with a thin peripheral layer of cytoplasm and a large central vacuole.

answer.text: Spherical, loosely arranged cells with dense cytoplasm filling the entire lumen and devoid of vacuoles
Heavily lignified, dead cells with thick secondary walls and obliterated lumens
Short collenchymatous cells with massive corner pectin thickenings and numerous chloroplasts
Elongated, compactly arranged cells with a small amount of cytoplasm lining the cell wall and a large central vacuole

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Definition and extent of the ground tissue system

questiontext.text: In flowering plants, the ground or fundamental tissue system comprises:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Plant Tissue Systems
Plant organs are divided into three primary systems based on morphology and spatial location: epidermal, ground (fundamental), and vascular.

Step 2: Delimitation of Ground Tissue
By definition, all tissues other than the epidermal tissue system and the conducting vascular bundles constitute the ground tissue system.

Final Answer:
Ground tissue encompasses all plant tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles.

answer.text: All internal tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles
Exclusively the xylem and phloem elements
Only the epidermis, cuticle, and epidermal trichomes
Exclusively the vascular cambium and cork cambium

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Identification of ground tissue in leaves

questiontext.text: In leaves, the ground tissue consists of thin-walled, chloroplast-containing cells and is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ground Tissue System of Foliar Organs
In leaves, the ground tissue occupies the region situated between the upper and lower epidermal layers.

Step 2: Nomenclature and Characteristics
This tissue is made of thin-walled parenchymatous cells rich in chloroplasts that perform photosynthesis, and is known as the mesophyll.

Final Answer:
The chloroplast-containing ground tissue in leaves is called the mesophyll.

answer.text: Endodermis
Mesophyll
Pericycle
Hypodermis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Parenchymatous ground tissue in primary plant axis

questiontext.text: In primary stems and roots, parenchymatous cells of the ground tissue system are typically present in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Components of Ground Tissue
Ground tissue makes up the bulk of the primary axis and is composed of simple tissues such as parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma.

Step 2: Spatial Zones in Primary Axis
In primary stems and roots, parenchyma cells form the cortex, pericycle, central pith, and radially oriented medullary rays.

Final Answer:
Parenchymatous ground tissue occurs in the cortex, pericycle, pith, and medullary rays of primary stems and roots.

answer.text: Tracheids, vessels, sieve tubes, and companion cells
Guard cells, subsidiary cells, trichomes, and root hairs
Cortex, pericycle, pith, and medullary rays
Bundle sheath cells, sieve tubes, and vessel elements

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Distinction between open and closed vascular bundles

questiontext.text: Vascular bundles that possess an intrafascicular cambium strip between xylem and phloem, giving them the capacity for secondary growth, are termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Cambium Presence
When a lateral meristematic tissue (cambium) is present between the primary phloem and primary xylem, secondary conducting elements can be generated.

Step 2: Terminology
Such bundles with active or potential secondary growth capacity are classified as open vascular bundles.

Final Answer:
Vascular bundles possessing cambium between xylem and phloem are called open vascular bundles.

answer.text: Closed vascular bundles
Radial vascular bundles
Concentric vascular bundles
Open vascular bundles

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q13 - Radial arrangement of vascular bundles in roots

questiontext.text: When primary xylem and primary phloem strands within a vascular cylinder are arranged in an alternate manner along different radii, the bundle arrangement is described as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Geometric Disposition of Conducting Tissues
Xylem and phloem can be arranged either together along the same radius or separately on distinct radii.

Step 2: Radial Pattern
When xylem and phloem patches lie alternately on separate radii, as is typical of roots, the arrangement is defined as radial.

Final Answer:
An alternate arrangement of xylem and phloem along different radii is called a radial vascular arrangement.

answer.text: Radial
Conjoint
Collateral
Concentric

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Characteristics of conjoint vascular bundles

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes a conjoint vascular bundle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Conjoint Bundles
In conjoint vascular bundles, both xylem and phloem are situated jointly along the same radial line.

Step 2: Relative Spatial Orientation
In stems and leaves where conjoint bundles occur, the phloem is typically oriented towards the outer (abaxial/peripheral) side, while the xylem is directed towards the interior (adaxial/pith) side.

Final Answer:
In conjoint vascular bundles, xylem and phloem are located along the same radius, with phloem positioned on the outer side of xylem.

answer.text: Xylem and phloem lie on alternating separate radii separated by parenchymatous conjunctive tissue
Xylem and phloem are situated along the same radius, with phloem usually located on the outer side of xylem
Phloem is located centrally while xylem completely surrounds it on all radii
Xylem and phloem are arranged along the same radius with xylem positioned external to phloem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q15 - Occurrence of closed vascular bundles in monocotyledons

questiontext.text: Why are the vascular bundles in monocotyledonous stems designated as 'closed'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Significance of Cambium
Cambium is the meristematic strip responsible for the secondary thickening of vascular tissues.

Step 2: Monocot Vascular Bundle Architecture
In monocots, no cambium exists between xylem and phloem within the bundle. Because they lack secondary developmental potential, these bundles are designated as closed.

Final Answer:
Monocot vascular bundles are termed closed because they lack cambium and do not produce secondary vascular tissues.

answer.text: They lack both xylem and phloem conducting elements
They are entirely sealed off from the ground tissue by a suberised endodermis
They lack cambium between xylem and phloem and cannot form secondary tissues
They possess an active cambium ring that ceases activity immediately after germination

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q16 - Anatomical features of epiblema in dicot roots

questiontext.text: In the transverse section of a young sunflower (dicot) root, the outermost layer is the epiblema, which is characterised by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structure of Epiblema (Piliferous Layer)
The epiblema (rhizodermis) represents the outermost single-layered covering of young dicot roots.

Step 2: Associated Features
Several epiblema cells extend outward as delicate unicellular root hairs to absorb soil water and minerals. It lacks stomata and cuticle to ensure permeability.

Final Answer:
The epiblema of dicot roots bears unicellular root hairs and lacks a cuticle.

answer.text: A heavy deposition of suberin forming Casparian strips
Multicellular branched trichomes with secretory tips
A thick layer of cuticle with numerous sunken stomata
Protrusion of epidermal cells into unicellular root hairs and lack of a waxy cuticle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q17 - Chemical composition and location of Casparian strips

questiontext.text: In the root endodermis of flowering plants, Casparian strips prevent the apoplastic flow of water. Which of the following accurately describes their chemical composition and the precise cellular walls on which they are deposited?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Root Endodermis Characteristics
The endodermis forms the innermost boundary of the root cortex, consisting of a continuous single layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces.

Step 2: Chemical Nature and Wall Deposition of Casparian Strips
Casparian strips consist of suberin, a waxy, water-impermeable substance. This suberin deposition occurs specifically on both the tangential walls and the radial walls of the endodermal cells.

Final Answer:
Casparian strips are composed of water-impermeable suberin deposited on both the tangential and radial walls of endodermal cells.

answer.text: Water-impermeable waxy suberin deposited on both tangential and radial walls of barrel-shaped cells
Water-permeable pectin deposited exclusively on the outer tangential walls of rounded cells
Lignin and cutin deposited solely on the inner tangential walls of collenchymatous cells
Suberin and cellulose deposited exclusively on the radial walls of intercellular spaces

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q18 - Developmental roles of pericycle in dicotyledonous roots

questiontext.text: In a primary dicotyledonous root, the pericycle consists of thick-walled parenchymatous cells. Which of the following developmental events directly originate from these pericycle cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Position of Pericycle
The pericycle lies directly inside the endodermis, surrounding the vascular cylinder in dicot roots.

Step 2: Developmental Fate
Cells of the root pericycle retain meristematic competence: they undergo dedifferentiation to initiate lateral root primordia and contribute to the formation of the vascular cambium during secondary growth.

Final Answer:
In dicot roots, the pericycle gives rise to lateral roots and participates in the formation of vascular cambium during secondary growth.

answer.text: Differentiation of primary protoxylem and metaxylem vessels
Initiation of lateral roots and part of the vascular cambium during secondary growth
Formation of the stomatal apparatus and glandular trichomes
Development of palisade parenchyma and spongy mesophyll

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q19 - Nature and location of conjunctive tissue in roots

questiontext.text: In the transverse section of a dicotyledonous root, the parenchymatous cells that lie in between the alternating xylem and phloem patches are referred to as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vascular Pattern of Dicot Root
The primary dicot root displays separate, radially arranged patches of primary xylem and primary phloem.

Step 2: Conjunctive Tissue Identity
The non-conducting ground parenchyma located in the interstitial regions between these separate xylem and phloem strands is specifically called conjunctive tissue.

Final Answer:
Parenchymatous cells between the xylem and phloem patches in a root constitute the conjunctive tissue.

answer.text: Medullary rays
Casparian strips
Conjunctive tissue
Starch sheath

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q20 - Xylem and phloem patch counts in dicot roots

questiontext.text: In the primary transverse section of a dicotyledonous root, how many xylem and phloem patches are typically present?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Xylem Architecture in Roots
Root steles are classified based on the number of radial xylem arches (diarch, triarch, tetrarch, polyarch).

Step 2: Condition in Dicot Roots
Dicot roots characteristically possess a limited number of xylem and phloem groups, usually ranging from two to four (diarch to tetrarch).

Final Answer:
Primary dicot roots typically have two to four xylem and phloem patches.

answer.text: More than six (polyarch)
Ten to twenty scattered bundles
Only a single central concentric patch
Two to four

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q21 - Tissues comprising the stele in primary roots

questiontext.text: In plant anatomy, all tissues situated on the inner side of the endodermis are collectively termed the stele. In a primary root, the stele therefore includes:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of the Stele
The stele constitutes the central core of the plant axis delimited externally by the endodermis.

Step 2: Components Inside the Endodermis
All tissues lying internal to the endodermis—namely the pericycle layer, the vascular tissues (xylem and phloem), and the central pith—collectively make up the stele.

Final Answer:
The stele comprises all tissues internal to the endodermis: pericycle, vascular bundles, and pith.

answer.text: Pericycle, vascular bundles, and pith
Cortex, endodermis, and pericycle
Epiblema, hypodermis, and cortex
Epidermis, Casparian strips, and medullary rays

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q22 - Developmental status of pith in dicot roots

questiontext.text: How is the central pith characterized in the transverse section of a primary dicotyledonous root?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomical Features of Dicot Root Core
In dicot roots, the metaxylem vessels often meet or closely approach the center.

Step 2: Pith Size
As a result of xylem convergence, the central parenchymatous pith in primary dicot roots is very small or inconspicuous.

Final Answer:
The pith in a primary dicot root is small or inconspicuous.

answer.text: Large and well developed
Small or inconspicuous
Completely hollow forming a prominent air cavity
Composed of heavily lignified sclerenchyma fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q23 - Polyarch xylem condition in monocot roots

questiontext.text: A botanist examining a transverse section of an unknown root observes more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles arranged alternately with phloem. This anatomical feature is characteristic of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Comparing Root Vascular Cylinders
Roots possess radial vascular bundles where xylem and phloem lie on alternate radii.

Step 2: Bundle Count Comparison
While dicot roots typically have 2 to 4 xylem bundles (diarch to tetrarch), monocot roots typically possess more than six xylem bundles, a state referred to as polyarch.

Final Answer:
Possession of more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles is a diagnostic feature of monocotyledonous roots.

answer.text: Dicotyledonous root
Dicotyledonous stem
Monocotyledonous root
Monocotyledonous stem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q24 - Pith development in monocot and dicot roots

questiontext.text: In contrast to the dicotyledonous root, the central pith in a monocotyledonous root is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pith in Dicot Roots
In dicot roots, the central core contains little parenchymatous tissue, leaving the pith small or inconspicuous.

Step 2: Pith in Monocot Roots
In monocot roots, the central parenchymatous region is extensive, prominent, and well developed.

Final Answer:
The pith of a monocot root is large and well developed, unlike the small or inconspicuous pith of a dicot root.

answer.text: Small and inconspicuous
Absent due to centripetal obliteration
Transformed into collenchymatous hypodermis
Large and well developed

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q25 - Secondary growth capacity in monocotyledonous roots

questiontext.text: Which of the following is true regarding secondary growth in monocotyledonous roots?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Meristematic Potential in Roots
Secondary growth requires the formation and activity of lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium).

Step 2: Monocot Root Anatomy
Monocot roots lack cambial meristems and do not develop any secondary vascular tissues; they do not undergo secondary growth.

Final Answer:
Monocotyledonous roots do not undergo any secondary growth.

answer.text: They do not undergo any secondary growth
They undergo extensive secondary growth through a continuous vascular cambium ring
They form secondary phloem only, without producing secondary xylem
Secondary growth occurs exclusively in their hypodermal zone

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q26 - Structure and function of hypodermis in dicot stem

questiontext.text: In the primary stem of a dicotyledonous plant, the hypodermis is located immediately below the epidermis and is composed of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Zonation of Dicot Stem Cortex
The cortex in a young dicot stem is differentiated into three sub-zones: hypodermis, cortical layers, and endodermis.

Step 2: Hypodermal Characteristics
The outer sub-zone, situated just beneath the epidermis, consists of a few layers of collenchymatous cells whose localized wall thickenings confer mechanical strength to the growing young stem.

Final Answer:
The hypodermis of a dicot stem consists of collenchymatous cells providing mechanical strength.

answer.text: A single layer of suberised barrel-shaped cells acting as a water barrier
A few layers of collenchymatous cells that provide mechanical strength
Several layers of dead sclerenchymatous fibres with narrow lumens
Thin-walled parenchymatous cells specialized for starch storage

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q27 - Characteristics of starch sheath in dicot stem

questiontext.text: In the dicotyledonous stem, the innermost layer of the cortex is referred to as the 'starch sheath' because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Innermost Cortical Layer
In dicot stems, the cortex terminates internally at the endodermis.

Step 2: Starch Sheath Designation
Because the cells of this endodermal layer are abundant in stored starch grains, it is specifically designated as the starch sheath.

Final Answer:
The endodermis in a dicot stem is termed the starch sheath because its cells are rich in starch grains.

answer.text: It is composed of pericyclic sclerenchyma cells synthesizing starch
It represents the hypodermis, which converts starch into chloroplasts
It represents the endodermis, whose cells are conspicuously rich in starch grains
It represents medullary rays that export starch radially to the cortex

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q28 - Pericycle architecture and composition in dicot stem

questiontext.text: In a transverse section of a young dicotyledonous stem, the pericycle is located on the inner side of the endodermis and occurs as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Location of Pericycle in Dicot Stem
The pericycle lies between the endodermis (starch sheath) and the vascular bundles.

Step 2: Morphology and Composition
Rather than forming a uniform parenchymatous sheath as in roots, the pericycle in a dicot stem occurs as distinctive semi-lunar patches of sclerenchymatous fibers positioned directly external to (above) each phloem strand.

Final Answer:
In a dicot stem, the pericycle exists as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma situated above the phloem.

answer.text: A continuous single-layered ring of suberised barrel-shaped cells
Radially oriented rows of thin-walled collenchyma between xylem bundles
A broad continuous zone of chlorenchymatous palisade tissue
Semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma positioned above the phloem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q29 - Location of medullary rays in dicot stems

questiontext.text: In a primary dicot stem, the radially placed parenchymatous cells present in the gaps between adjacent vascular bundles constitute the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vascular Pattern of Dicot Stem
Vascular bundles in dicot stems are arranged in a ring separated by non-vascular parenchymatous tracts.

Step 2: Medullary Rays
These radially oriented columns of parenchymatous cells interconnecting the central pith with the cortex are termed medullary rays.

Final Answer:
Radially placed parenchymatous cells between vascular bundles in a dicot stem constitute medullary rays.

answer.text: Medullary rays
Bundle sheath extensions
Casparian strips
Conjunctive tissue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q30 - Ring arrangement of vascular bundles in dicot stem

questiontext.text: The arrangement of vascular bundles in the form of a organized ring is a diagnostic anatomical characteristic of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Comparison of Stem Anatomy
In monocot stems, vascular bundles are irregularly scattered throughout the ground tissue.

Step 2: Dicot Stem Diagnostic Feature
In dicot stems, vascular bundles are characteristically arranged in an orderly circular ring surrounding the pith.

Final Answer:
A ring arrangement of vascular bundles is a hallmark characteristic of dicotyledonous stems.

answer.text: Monocotyledonous stem
Dicotyledonous stem
Monocotyledonous root
Dicotyledonous root

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q31 - Complete vascular bundle profile of a dicot stem

questiontext.text: Which of the following combinations of features accurately describes each vascular bundle in a young dicotyledonous stem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Bundle Morphology
In dicot stems, xylem and phloem occur along the same radius, which defines them as conjoint.

Step 2: Cambium Status
A strip of intrafascicular cambium is present between xylem and phloem, rendering them open for secondary growth.

Step 3: Protoxylem Orientation
In stems, the earliest formed xylem (protoxylem) lies towards the interior/center while metaxylem lies towards the periphery, which is the endarch condition.

Final Answer:
Vascular bundles of a dicot stem are conjoint, open, and feature endarch protoxylem.

answer.text: Conjoint, closed, and with exarch protoxylem
Radial, open, and with endarch protoxylem
Conjoint, open, and with endarch protoxylem
Radial, closed, and with exarch protoxylem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q32 - Anatomy of the central pith in dicot stems

questiontext.text: In a primary dicotyledonous stem, the central portion of the axis is occupied by the pith, which consists of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Position and Extent of Pith
The pith (medulla) occupies the central core of the dicot stem, interior to the ring of vascular bundles.

Step 2: Cellular Composition
It is composed of numerous rounded, living parenchymatous cells featuring noticeable intercellular spaces that facilitate gas diffusion and metabolic storage.

Final Answer:
The pith of a dicot stem is composed of rounded parenchymatous cells with prominent intercellular spaces.

answer.text: Compactly packed collenchymatous cells with thickened pectin corners
Heavily lignified, dead sclerenchymatous fibres forming a rigid cylinder
A hollow cavity surrounded by a single layer of endodermal cells
A large number of rounded parenchymatous cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q33 - Nature of hypodermis in monocotyledonous stems

questiontext.text: The hypodermis of a monocotyledonous stem differs anatomically from that of a dicotyledonous stem in being:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Hypodermis in Dicot Stem
In dicot stems, the hypodermis is collenchymatous, providing flexible mechanical support.

Step 2: Hypodermis in Monocot Stem
In monocot stems, the hypodermis is composed of thick-walled, lignified sclerenchyma cells to provide rigid structural support.

Final Answer:
The hypodermis of a monocot stem is sclerenchymatous.

answer.text: Sclerenchymatous
Collenchymatous
Parenchymatous
Suberised

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q34 - Vascular bundle arrangement in monocot stem

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of anatomical characteristics is uniquely found in a monocotyledonous stem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Bundle Distribution in Monocot Stem
Unlike the ring arrangement of dicot stems, vascular bundles in monocot stems are numerous and scattered throughout the ground tissue.

Step 2: Bundle Sheath Structure
Each individual vascular bundle is enclosed by a protective sheath of sclerenchymatous fibers, known as the bundle sheath.

Final Answer:
Monocot stems possess scattered vascular bundles each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath.

answer.text: Vascular bundles arranged in a neat ring, each capped by parenchymatous medullary rays
Scattered vascular bundles, each enveloped by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath
Vascular bundles alternating radially and surrounded by Casparian strips
Vascular bundles restricted strictly to a single sub-epidermal circle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q35 - Size comparison of vascular bundles in monocot stem

questiontext.text: When examining the transverse section of a monocotyledonous stem, how do the peripheral vascular bundles compare in size to the centrally located ones?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Distribution Pattern of Monocot Stem Bundles
The vascular bundles are scattered across the parenchymatous ground tissue with higher density near the periphery.

Step 2: Size Gradient
As an anatomical adaptation, the bundles located near the periphery are characteristically smaller and more crowded, whereas those positioned towards the center are larger and more widely spaced.

Final Answer:
In a monocot stem, peripheral vascular bundles are generally smaller than centrally located ones.

answer.text: Peripheral vascular bundles are generally much larger than the centrally located ones
All vascular bundles are strictly identical in diameter across the entire cross-section
Peripheral vascular bundles are generally smaller than the centrally located ones
Peripheral vascular bundles are open, while centrally located bundles are closed

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q36 - Phloem tissue composition in monocotyledonous stems

questiontext.text: Which constituent of complex vascular tissues is characteristically absent in the vascular bundles of a monocotyledonous stem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Composition of Phloem
Angiosperm phloem typically consists of sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem fibres, and phloem parenchyma.

Step 2: Specific Absence in Monocots
In the vascular bundles of monocot stems, phloem parenchyma is characteristically absent, while sieve tubes and companion cells remain present.

Final Answer:
Phloem parenchyma is absent in the vascular bundles of monocotyledonous stems.

answer.text: Companion cells
Sieve tubes
Xylem vessels
Phloem parenchyma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q37 - Occurrence of water cavities within vascular bundles

questiontext.text: The presence of water-containing cavities (lysigenous cavities) within each vascular bundle is an anatomical hallmark of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vascular Bundle Anatomy in Monocot Stem
In monocot stems, the breakdown of protoxylem elements during rapid elongation creates a distinct cavity within the bundle.

Step 2: Diagnostic Feature
These water-containing lacunae (protoxylem cavities) are found inside the vascular bundles of monocot stems.

Final Answer:
Water-containing cavities within vascular bundles are characteristic of monocotyledonous stems.

answer.text: Monocotyledonous stem
Dicotyledonous stem
Dicotyledonous root
Dorsiventral leaf

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q38 - Organization of ground tissue in monocot stems

questiontext.text: Regarding the ground tissue system in a monocotyledonous stem, which of the following statements is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ground Tissue Structure in Monocot Stem
In monocot stems, vascular bundles are scattered randomly throughout the cross-section.

Step 2: Lack of Zonation
Because of this scattered bundle distribution, the ground tissue remains an undifferentiated, large parenchymatous matrix without distinct cortical, pericyclic, endodermal, or medullary boundaries.

Final Answer:
In a monocot stem, the ground tissue is a large, conspicuous parenchymatous mass not differentiated into distinct cortical zones or pith.

answer.text: It is sharply divided into a distinct cortex, starch sheath, and semi-lunar pericyclic patches
It forms a large, conspicuous parenchymatous mass that is not differentiated into cortex, endodermis, pericycle, and pith
It is composed entirely of dead sclerenchymatous stone cells without intercellular spaces
It contains medullary rays that radiate outward from a well-defined central pith

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q39 - Stomatal frequency on surfaces of dorsiventral leaves

questiontext.text: In the vertical section of a typical dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf, stomatal distribution is characterised by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomy of Dorsiventral Leaf Epidermis
A dorsiventral leaf displays clear structural differences between its upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) surfaces.

Step 2: Stomatal Density
The abaxial epidermis bears a significantly higher number of stomata than the adaxial epidermis. The adaxial surface may even lack stomata entirely to minimize direct evaporative water loss from sunlight exposure.

Final Answer:
In a dorsiventral leaf, the abaxial epidermis typically bears more stomata than the adaxial epidermis.

answer.text: Equal numbers of stomata on both the adaxial and abaxial surfaces
A complete absence of stomata on the abaxial surface
More stomata on the abaxial (lower) epidermis than on the adaxial (upper) epidermis
Stomata restricted exclusively to the adaxial epidermis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q40 - Cellular characteristics and orientation of palisade parenchyma

questiontext.text: In a dorsiventral leaf, the palisade parenchyma is situated adaxially and is composed of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Differentiation of Leaf Mesophyll
The mesophyll in dicot leaves is divided into two distinct zones: palisade parenchyma and spongy parenchyma.

Step 2: Palisade Parenchyma Architecture
The palisade layer is positioned towards the upper (adaxial) epidermis and consists of vertically elongated, columnar cells that are tightly packed and aligned parallel to one another to maximize light absorption.

Final Answer:
Palisade parenchyma consists of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other on the adaxial side of the leaf.

answer.text: Loosely arranged oval cells with large intercellular air spaces
Thick-walled lignified cells lacking chloroplasts
Barrel-shaped cells with suberin bands on their radial walls
Elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q41 - Structural features of spongy parenchyma in dicot leaves

questiontext.text: In the mesophyll of a dorsiventral leaf, the spongy parenchyma is characterised by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Position of Spongy Parenchyma
Spongy parenchyma is located beneath the palisade layer, extending downwards to the lower (abaxial) epidermis.

Step 2: Cellular Arrangement
Its cells are oval or spherical and arranged loosely, creating numerous spacious intercellular spaces and air chambers that facilitate gas exchange between stomata and photosynthetic cells.

Final Answer:
Spongy parenchyma consists of loosely arranged oval or round cells with large intercellular spaces and air cavities.

answer.text: Oval or rounded cells arranged loosely with numerous large spaces and air cavities
Columnar cells packed tightly without any intercellular spaces
Dead cells with heavy spiral secondary wall lignification
Large, empty, colourless cells that regulate leaf rolling

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q42 - Characteristics of bundle sheath cells enclosing leaf veins

questiontext.text: In the transverse section of a dorsiventral leaf, each vascular bundle embedded within the veins is surrounded by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vascular Bundles in Foliar Veins
The vascular bundles in leaves are embedded in the mesophyll along the veins and midrib.

Step 2: Sheath Enclosure
Every vascular bundle is directly enveloped by a protective sheath comprising a layer of tightly fitted, thick-walled cells known as bundle sheath cells.

Final Answer:
Leaf vascular bundles are enclosed by a layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells.

answer.text: A ring of thin-walled bulliform cells
A layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells
A single layer of barrel-shaped endodermal cells with Casparian strips
A semi-lunar cap of dead collenchymatous fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q43 - Orientation of vascular tissues in dorsiventral leaf

questiontext.text: In a vertical section of a dorsiventral leaf, what is the relative spatial orientation of xylem and phloem within each vascular bundle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Orientation of Conjoint Bundles in Leaves
Leaf vascular traces represent direct continuations of the stem's conjoint collateral bundles where xylem is internal (towards the axis center) and phloem is external.

Step 2: Resulting Foliar Position
When diverging into the leaf blade, the internal xylem aligns towards the upper or adaxial surface, whereas the external phloem faces the lower or abaxial surface.

Final Answer:
In leaf vascular bundles, xylem is oriented towards the adaxial epidermis and phloem towards the abaxial epidermis.

answer.text: Phloem faces towards the adaxial (upper) epidermis, while xylem faces towards the abaxial (lower) epidermis
Xylem is arranged in a peripheral ring completely enclosing a central core of phloem
Xylem faces towards the adaxial (upper) epidermis, while phloem faces towards the abaxial (lower) epidermis
Xylem and phloem alternate with each other along separate vertical radii

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q44 - Venation effect on vascular bundles in dicot leaf

questiontext.text: In a dorsiventral leaf, the sizes of the vascular bundles seen in a transverse section vary considerably because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Venation Pattern in Dicot Leaves
Dicot leaves exhibit reticulate venation, producing a branching network of veins of varying calibers, with the thickest vein at the midrib and progressively finer veinlets branching through the lamina.

Step 2: Consequence for Bundle Dimensions
Because the size of a vascular bundle is directly proportional to the thickness of the vein housing it, bundles seen in a transverse section exhibit marked variation in size.

Final Answer:
Vascular bundle sizes vary in a dicot leaf because the veins of reticulate venation vary in thickness.

answer.text: Some bundles lack xylem vessels while others lack phloem elements
Peripheral bundles possess secondary cambium while central bundles do not
Bulliform cells compress the smaller bundles near the stomatal pores
The reticulate venation involves veins that vary significantly in thickness across the lamina

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q45 - Mesophyll organization in isobilateral leaves

questiontext.text: An anatomical feature that clearly differentiates an isobilateral (monocotyledonous) leaf from a dorsiventral leaf is that in an isobilateral leaf:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dicot versus Monocot Leaf Mesophyll
In dicot (dorsiventral) leaves, the photosynthetic mesophyll is bifurcated into upper palisade parenchyma and lower spongy parenchyma.

Step 2: Isobilateral Leaf Condition
In monocot (isobilateral) leaves, both surfaces receive roughly equal sunlight; consequently, the mesophyll remains uniform and undifferentiated into palisade and spongy zones.

Final Answer:
In an isobilateral leaf, the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma.

answer.text: The mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma
The mesophyll consists entirely of dead sclerenchyma cells
Stomata are completely restricted to the upper epidermis only
Vascular bundles lack bundle sheath cells entirely

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q46 - Origin and cellular characteristics of bulliform cells

questiontext.text: In grasses, bulliform cells are formed by the modification of which specific cells, and what are their cytological features?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Origin of Bulliform Cells
Bulliform cells differentiate directly from the epidermis of the leaf.

Step 2: Spatial Location and Features
In grasses, certain epidermal cells on the upper (adaxial) surface along the veins enlarge and lose their chloroplasts, becoming large, empty, and colourless.

Final Answer:
Bulliform cells are modified adaxial epidermal cells along veins that are large, empty, and colourless.

answer.text: Abaxial epidermal cells modifying into small, chloroplast-rich guard cells
Certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins modifying into large, empty, colourless cells
Spongy mesophyll cells modifying into thick-walled lignified storage cells
Bundle sheath cells modifying into elongated starch-accumulating cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q47 - Inward leaf curling mechanism governed by bulliform cells

questiontext.text: During severe water stress, how do bulliform cells in grass leaves bring about inward leaf curling to minimize water loss?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Turgid State of Bulliform Cells
When adequate water is available, bulliform cells absorb moisture, become turgid, and expand, exposing the broad leaf surface for sunlight interception.

Step 2: Flaccid Response under Stress
Under drought or water deficit, these cells lose water and turn flaccid. The resulting loss of turgor pressure causes the blade to curl or roll inwards, shielding the stomata and minimizing transpiration.

Final Answer:
When bulliform cells become flaccid due to water loss during drought, the leaf curls inward to minimise water loss.

answer.text: They absorb water and become turgid, actively bending the leaf inward
They undergo rapid mitotic divisions that fold the leaf margin
They become flaccid due to water loss, causing the leaf lamina to roll inwards
They deposit heavy suberin layers on both epidermal surfaces

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q48 - Parallel venation effect on leaf vascular bundles

questiontext.text: In the vertical section of an isobilateral (monocotyledonous) leaf, the vascular bundles (except in main veins) are of nearly similar sizes. This anatomical uniformity is a direct reflection of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Monocot Leaf Venation
Monocot leaves characteristically possess parallel venation, wherein veins run parallel along the length of the lamina without a tapering reticulate meshwork.

Step 2: Effect on Bundle Dimensions
Because the parallel veins are of roughly equal diameter throughout the leaf blade (aside from the principal central veins), cross sections reveal vascular bundles that are remarkably uniform in size.

Final Answer:
Near-similar sizes of vascular bundles in monocot leaves directly reflect the parallel venation pattern.

answer.text: The presence of open vascular bundles with active secondary growth
The differentiation of mesophyll into palisade and spongy layers
The total absence of bundle sheath cells around all veinlets
The parallel venation pattern characteristic of monocot leaves
